Battle of Midway. Fought from June fourth to seventh, nineteen forty-two, the Battle of Midway stands as the turning point of the Pacific War. American naval forces, warned by intelligence of Japanese intentions, ambushed the enemy fleet and sank four irreplaceable fleet carriers while losing only one, permanently shifting naval superiority to the United States and ending Japanese strategic initiative in the Pacific.

The battle centered on Midway Atoll, roughly equidistant between Hawaii and Japan's earlier conquests, and lasted four days of intense carrier warfare. The American victory sank four Japanese fleet carriers—Akagi, Kaga, Soryu, and Hiryu—and one heavy cruiser. The U.S. lost one fleet carrier, the Yorktown. Japanese forces were commanded by Admiral Isoroku Yamamoto, while American forces were under Admiral Chester Nimitz and tactical commanders including Admiral Frank Jack Fletcher.

The American victory was decided by codebreakers who decrypted Japanese plans, allowing Nimitz to position his carriers in ambush before the Japanese even learned of their location. The battle destroyed the cream of Japanese naval aviation—experienced pilots who were irreplaceable. Subsequent Japanese carriers carried less-trained aircrews, permanently degrading Japanese combat effectiveness. This battle marked the end of Japanese expansion. Thereafter, Japan fought a defensive war of attrition across the Pacific, unable to recapture the initiative against an opponent strengthened by industrial might and intelligence advantage.
